Time feels like the one thing we all understand. It's much stranger than that.

Number one.

scene.title: YOU ARE LOOKING AT THE PAST

lines.text: Light is the fastest thing in the universe. But it still takes time to get anywhere.
Sunlight needs about eight minutes to cross the roughly one hundred and fifty million kilometers between the Sun and Earth.
lines.caption: Sunlight needs about 8 minutes to cross the roughly 150 million kilometers between the Sun and Earth.

lines.text: So when you see the Sun, you're seeing it as it was eight minutes ago. If it suddenly vanished, you wouldn't know for eight more minutes.
lines.caption: So when you see the Sun, you're seeing it as it was 8 minutes ago. If it suddenly vanished, you wouldn't know for 8 more minutes.

lines.text: Even the Moon you see is about one second old.
lines.caption: Even the Moon you see is about 1 second old.

lines.text: Now go farther. On a dark night, you can spot a faint smudge called the Andromeda galaxy.
The light hitting your eyes from it left about two and a half million years ago.
lines.caption: The light hitting your eyes from it left about 2.5 million years ago.

lines.text: Look at almost any star tonight, and you may be seeing light that left it before you were born.
Every time you look up at night, you're not seeing space. You're seeing its history.
Number two.

scene.title: A DAY LONGER THAN A YEAR

lines.text: On Venus, a single spin takes about two hundred and forty-three Earth days.
lines.caption: On Venus, a single spin takes about 243 Earth days.

lines.text: But one trip around the Sun takes only about two hundred and twenty-five.
lines.caption: But one trip around the Sun takes only about 225.

lines.text: So Venus finishes a whole year before it finishes turning around once.
Think about that. On Venus, you could celebrate a birthday, and it would still be the very same day.
And it spins backwards compared to Earth. On Venus, the Sun rises in the west.
Number three.
For centuries, Britain used an old calendar that added leap days a little too often. So, over the centuries, the dates slowly drifted out of step with the seasons.
The first countries in Europe had already fixed this back in fifteen eighty-two. Britain held out for almost two hundred years.
lines.caption: The first countries in Europe had already fixed this back in 1582. Britain held out for almost 200 years.

lines.text: To fix it in one go, Britain and its colonies simply skipped eleven days.
lines.caption: To fix it in one go, Britain and its colonies simply skipped 11 days.

lines.text: People went to bed on Wednesday, the second of September, seventeen fifty-two. And woke up on Thursday, the fourteenth.
lines.caption: People went to bed on Wednesday, September 2, 1752. And woke up on Thursday, the 14th.

lines.text: You may have heard that angry crowds rioted, shouting give us our eleven days. Historians say there's very little evidence that ever happened.
lines.caption: You may have heard that angry crowds rioted, shouting "Give us our 11 days!" Historians say there's very little evidence that ever happened.

lines.text: But the missing days were real. Look up a British calendar for that month, and they're simply not there.
That September had just nineteen days. Imagine paying a full month's rent for that.
lines.caption: That September had just 19 days. Imagine paying a full month's rent for that.

lines.text: Number four.
February has twenty-eight days, or twenty-nine in a leap year. Except once, in Sweden.
lines.caption: February has 28 days, or 29 in a leap year. Except once, in Sweden.

lines.text: Sweden tried to switch to the new calendar slowly, by skipping leap days one at a time. The plan got muddled, and the country ended up out of step with everyone.
So in seventeen twelve, Sweden gave up and went back to the old calendar by adding two leap days in one year.
lines.caption: So in 1712, Sweden gave up and went back to the old calendar by adding two leap days in one year.

lines.text: And that's how February the thirtieth became a real date. It even appears in Swedish church records.
lines.caption: And that's how February 30 became a real date. It even appears in Swedish church records.

lines.text: A day that never existed anywhere else, before or since.
Number five.

scene.title: THE ISLAND THAT SKIPPED A FRIDAY

lines.text: In the middle of the Pacific runs an invisible line called the International Date Line. Cross it, and the date changes.
Before the switch, Samoa was almost a whole day behind its closest neighbors.
In twenty eleven, the island nation of Samoa decided to jump to the other side of that line, to share the same days as its big trading partners, Australia and New Zealand.
lines.caption: In 2011, the island nation of Samoa decided to jump to the other side of that line, to share the same days as its big trading partners, Australia and New Zealand.

lines.text: So the country went from Thursday, the twenty-ninth of December, straight to Saturday, the thirty-first.
lines.caption: So the country went from Thursday, December 29, straight to Saturday, the 31st.

lines.text: Friday, the thirtieth of December, twenty eleven, never happened in Samoa. Anyone with a birthday that day simply didn't get one.
lines.caption: Friday, December 30, 2011, never happened in Samoa. Anyone with a birthday that day simply didn't get one.

lines.text: Number six.
We tend to think of the Aztecs as ancient, and universities as modern. Here's the twist.
There was already teaching at Oxford, in England, by the year ten ninety-six.
lines.caption: There was already teaching at Oxford, in England, by the year 1096.

lines.text: The Aztec capital, Tenochtitlan, wasn't founded until about thirteen twenty-five. More than two centuries later.

lines.text: So when the Aztec capital was just being built on a lake in Mexico, students in Oxford were already walking to class. And Oxford is still teaching students today.
Number seven.
The Great Pyramid of Giza was finished about four and a half thousand years ago.
lines.caption: The Great Pyramid of Giza was finished about 4,500 years ago.

lines.text: You'd think woolly mammoths were long gone by then. They weren't.
A small group survived on Wrangel Island, in the Arctic Ocean north of Siberia, until about four thousand years ago.
lines.caption: A small group survived on Wrangel Island, in the Arctic Ocean north of Siberia, until about 4,000 years ago.

lines.text: When the last mammoth died, the Great Pyramid was already centuries old.

Ancient Egypt lasted so long that it had its own ancient history.
The Great Pyramid was built around two thousand five hundred and sixty BC.
lines.caption: The Great Pyramid was built around 2560 BC.

lines.text: Cleopatra, the last ruler of ancient Egypt, died in thirty BC. Already about two and a half thousand years later.

Number nine.
In movies, dinosaurs all seem to live together. In reality, the age of dinosaurs lasted an enormous stretch of time.
Stegosaurus roamed North America about one hundred and fifty million years ago.
lines.caption: Stegosaurus roamed North America about 150 million years ago.

Number ten. The one I promised.

scene.title: YOUR HEAD IS OLDER THAN YOUR FEET

lines.text: Einstein predicted that time runs a little faster the farther you are from Earth's gravity. Even a few centimeters farther.
In twenty ten, scientists at the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology tested it with two of the most precise clocks ever built.
lines.caption: In 2010, scientists at the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) tested it with two of the most precise clocks ever built.

lines.text: They raised one clock by just thirty-three centimeters, about one foot. And it really did tick faster.
lines.caption: They raised one clock by just 33 centimeters, about one foot. And it really did tick faster.

lines.text: The difference is tiny. Over a whole lifetime, it adds up to about ninety billionths of a second.

lines.caption: The difference is tiny. Over a whole lifetime, it adds up to about 90 billionths of a second.

lines.text: But it's real. Your head sits higher than your feet, so your head is aging just a tiny bit faster.
Walk up a flight of stairs, and your clock speeds up. Just very, very slightly.
And this isn't just a lab trick. Your phone depends on it. G P S satellites fly about twenty thousand kilometers up, where gravity is weaker.
lines.caption: And this isn't just a lab trick. Your phone depends on it. GPS satellites fly about 20,000 kilometers up, where gravity is weaker.

lines.text: Their clocks run fast by about thirty-eight millionths of a second every day.
lines.caption: Their clocks run fast by about 38 millionths of a second every day.

lines.text: If engineers didn't correct for that, your map's position errors would grow by about ten kilometers every single day.

lines.text: So every time your phone finds you on a map, it's quietly proving that time itself bends.
